correctness.rationale: Brunn–Minkowski gives the midpoint body area at least the common area, while inclusion in the equal-area middle body gives the reverse inequality. Equality therefore holds, so the two outer convex bodies are homothetic; equal area forces a translation, and equal-area inclusion identifies the middle body with the midpoint translate. An affine shear turns all three slices into copies of one body \(K\). For any nonhorizontal halfspace containing the middle centroid, its slice sections are nested parallel halfplanes; the middle one contains the centroid and therefore at least \(4/9\) of \(K\), and one outer section contains it and contributes at least another \(4/9\). Horizontal halfspaces contain at least two whole slices. Thus the captured mass is at least \(8a/9=(8/27)\cdot3a\).

evidence: Theorem 1 covers arbitrary slice areas and guarantees \(2/9\), which is sharp globally.
Its sharpness example has slice areas tending to \(0,1/2,1/2\), so it does not dominate the equal-area subclass.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The universal theorem is broader in hypotheses but strictly weaker in conclusion. It cannot imply the improved \(8/27\) depth under exact balance.

final_claim: If three planar convex bodies have equal positive area and satisfy \(\tfrac12(A_0+A_2)\subseteq A_1\), then they are translates in arithmetic progression, and the centroid of the middle slice has three-slice halfspace depth at least \(8/27\) of total mass.
limitations: The bound \(8/27\) is not proved optimal.
Exact equality of the three slice areas is essential to the rigidity argument; no near-balance stability estimate is proved.
